details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Azimuth: Interplanetary Guide is a website that gives an astronaut on Mars one navigable, layered map of Jezero Crater, showing the safest route and always the way home. Tagline: "Know the way home."

An astronaut walking on Mars has to answer three questions at the same time: can I go this way, will my suit hold, and how do I get back if something fails? Today that means reading separate maps, doing calculations by hand and keeping the whole route in mind. Azimuth answers all three on a single screen.

The experience opens with a 3D, interactive Mars that the user can rotate and zoom, with a "You are here" marker on Jezero Crater. From there the camera dives into a web map of Jezero. The user can drag and zoom it, switch NASA data layers on and off, and click markers. The flow then follows seven steps:

1. Plan. The astronaut draws a route by clicking the map, or asks the Azimuth AI assistant by text or voice ("take me to the delta"). The assistant traces the route options on the map.

2. Route dossier. The site reads every data layer along the route and summarizes it in one panel: elevation and slope, surface temperature (day or night), minerals, geologic units, hazards on the way, estimated radiation and near-surface air data. An elevation profile shows the climbs, and science targets along the route (sample sites such as Three Forks Sample Depot or Enchanted Lake) can be added as stops.

3. Check against the suit. The site compares the route with the suit's temperature range, remaining oxygen and battery. A section that is too cold or too steep, or that the oxygen left can't cover, becomes an alert at that exact spot.

4. Alerts. Hazards are always visible in a dedicated color, and each alert says what to do, not only what it is (for example: "Scarp tens of metres high: approach from the base and climb only via a ramp").

5. Route options. Up to three options are shown side by side (safest, balanced, fastest), each with distance, time, oxygen left on return and number of alerts. The astronaut chooses.

6. Walk. A walking view shows the position on the route, what is ahead (distances, headings, upcoming hazards), a mission clock, and the real Perseverance photo nearest to the next segment, with the current temperature and slope ahead.

7. Rescue. One large button, available from every screen, switches the interface to Rescue mode. It shows the return route to the shelter (the Perseverance landing site, Octavia E. Butler Landing), the distance and time to get there, the oxygen needed with a safety margin versus the oxygen available, and the point of no return: the point where the remaining oxygen only covers the trip back.

Under the hood, routes are computed with a cost map built from slope, mapped hazards, cold and proximity to the real Perseverance track. A least-cost path search (A*) then finds the options. Oxygen, autonomy and point-of-no-return calculations come from the suit parameters (oxygen consumption per hour, walking speed, thermal range).

The Azimuth AI assistant sits at the center of the experience. It traces routes on request, compares options, explains each alert in one sentence, answers questions such as "how much oxygen margin do I have?", and talks to support robots (asking a scout to check the path, calling the rescue transport). Three rules keep it safe:

(1) It never calculates on its own. It calls the site's own functions and explains the results, so it cannot invent numbers.

(2) It suggests, and the astronaut confirms before any action.

(3) When data is missing, it says so.

NASA DATA USED (eight types, all open)

- Optical imagery: MRO CTX mosaic of Jezero at 6 m per pixel, the base of the map.

- Elevation: MOLA and the CTX digital terrain model, used for slope along the route and for the route cost.

- Thermal: THEMIS infrared, day and night, used as an approximate surface temperature (thermal brightness) and compared with the suit's range.

- Minerals: CRISM, showing carbonates and clays, used for science stops.

- Geology: USGS Astrogeology geologic maps and dune data, used for hazard and terrain context.

- Landforms: named landforms of Jezero from NASA Mars Trek (delta front, channels, breach, dune fields), used as hazard zones.

- Atmosphere: Perseverance MEDA air temperature and pressure, shown in the panel.

- Radiation: Curiosity RAD surface dose, used as an estimate (Perseverance carries no dose detector) and labeled as such.

On top of these, the real Perseverance traverse is drawn on the map, and suggested routes prefer sections a rover has already crossed safely. Real raw images from Perseverance (Mastcam-Z, Navcam) are linked to points along the route. Map layers come from NASA Mars Trek as map tiles, and rover photos from the Perseverance raw images feed (credit NASA/JPL-Caltech).

BENEFITS

- One place for the decisions that matter: where to walk, whether the suit holds and how to return.

- Less mental load. The assistant does the calculations, so the astronaut's attention stays on the terrain.

- Hazards appear before they become emergencies, and every alert comes with an action.

- The way home is always one tap away, with the point of no return made explicit.

- Routes are grounded in real orbital data and real rover experience, not in guesses.

- Designed for gloves and a visor: large buttons, high contrast, critical alerts always on screen, Rescue reachable from any screen.

INTENDED IMPACT

- For the astronaut: safer, faster decisions during surface walks, with a clear return plan at every moment.

- For mission planning: routes can be compared quickly with real orbital data and rover tracks before anyone leaves the base.

- Beyond Mars: the same method (layered orbital data, a cost map, suit constraints and a return-first design) works for any place with orbital maps, such as the Moon.

- For the public and education: anyone can explore Jezero Crater on a navigable map with real NASA data and real rover photos, in English or Portuguese, with an interactive tutorial.

This impact is potential: the demo uses simulated suit data and has not been tested with astronauts.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

- Language: TypeScript.

- Web app: Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, with zustand for state.

- Map: Leaflet / react-leaflet, using the planet's degrees directly as map coordinates, with the CTX mosaic over NASA Mars Trek tiles.

- 3D opening: Three.js with React Three Fiber and drei, with a textured Mars globe.

- AI: Google Gemini via @google/genai with function calling. The API key stays on the server (a Next.js API route), with a per-IP rate limit. An offline "Plan B" answers with pre-written responses that use the same real calculations, so the demo also works without a network connection.

- Data processing: Node scripts with tsx, sharp and geotiff to convert the CTX GeoTIFF and the elevation and thermal rasters into web images and numeric grids for slope, temperature, hazards and track proximity.

- Voice: Web Speech API for spoken questions and spoken replies.

- Testing: Vitest for the route, oxygen, rescue and offline-AI logic.

- Design: Figma (flowchart, design system and screens).

- Deployment: Vercel.

- Hardware: none beyond the team's laptops. Suit telemetry is simulated with sliders in the demo, where a real suit would feed its own sensors.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It is designed around the return, not only the destination: the point of no return and the shelter route are first-class features, not an afterthought.

- It turns orbital data into decisions. Instead of showing layers for their own sake, it reads them along the route and translates them into "go", "careful" or "do this instead".

- It connects the astronaut to the robots already on Mars: routes prefer real rover tracks, real rover photos show what lies ahead, and support robots (scout, carrier, relay, beacon, depot, rescue transport) appear as a concept the assistant can coordinate.

- The AI is constrained by design: it explains, it never calculates numbers itself, and it always asks for confirmation.

- The experience is cinematic and practical at the same time: a 3D Mars that dives into a working mission map, with a mission-blueprint look built for gloved hands.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

- Safety first: always-visible alerts, Rescue from every screen, a safety margin on oxygen, and confirmation before any action.

- Honesty about data: every simulated number is labeled "SAMPLE DATA". Surface temperature is marked as approximate (THEMIS thermal brightness), radiation as an estimate from Curiosity RAD, and support robots as a concept. Every image and dataset is credited.

- Usability in a suit: large touch targets, high contrast, short alert messages, voice input.

- Reliability: offline map tiles and the AI's offline Plan B, so the demo does not depend on the network. API keys never reach the browser, and rate limiting protects the public link.

- Accessibility and reach: English by default with a Portuguese option, a responsive layout (collapsible panels on desktop, a bottom drawer on phones), an About screen and a 15-step interactive tutorial.

- Scope: a website rather than an app, so it could be built and shared within the hackathon weekend.

- Challenge requirements: at least three NASA data types (we use eight), safety first, routes that avoid obstacles, and photos from the rovers' point of view.
